body:
What makes a Jain temple a structural monument?

A structural Jain temple is built by assembling construction materials rather than by excavating an enclosed space from a rock mass. Such temples commonly contain a principal shrine housing an image of a Tirthankara, together with halls, corridors, subsidiary shrines and architectural decoration.

The inner shrine is often called the garbhagriha, while a pillared assembly hall is known as a mandapa. A tower or shikhara may rise above the principal shrine. These terms are also used in descriptions of Hindu temple architecture because regional building traditions shared structural forms.

The presence of a garbhagriha, mandapa or shikhara does not, by itself, establish a temple's religious affiliation. The main image, inscriptions and other associated symbols are essential for identifying it as a Jain temple.

Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill

Palitana, near Bhavnagar in Gujarat, is one of the most important Jain pilgrimage centres. The temples occupy Shatrunjaya Hill and form a large group of shrines rather than a single isolated building.

The principal religious association of the complex is with Adinatha or Rishabhanatha, the 1st Tirthankara. The site contains numerous enclosed temple groups and richly carved structures. Its development extended over many centuries, with successive phases of construction, repair and addition.

Architecturally, Palitana illustrates how a sacred hill could become a concentrated temple landscape. Paths, enclosed groups of shrines and successive courtyards organise movement through the complex. The presence of many temples does not mean that they were constructed at the same date or by one patron.

Girnar and the Neminatha temple

Girnar, near Junagadh in Gujarat, contains important Jain and Hindu sacred monuments. Among its Jain shrines, the Neminatha Temple is especially significant. Neminatha is the 22nd Tirthankara, whose identifying emblem is the conch.

The Neminatha Temple complex preserves substantial medieval Jain architecture. The association of Girnar with Neminatha is a central fact for identifying the site's Jain heritage.

Taranga and the Ajitanatha temple

Taranga Hill, in the Mehsana region of Gujarat, is an important Jain religious and architectural centre. Its principal Jain temple is dedicated to Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara.

The surviving main temple is associated with the 12th-century Chaulukya or Solanki period and the patronage of Kumarapala. It provides a Gujarat example of the developed structural temple tradition, with a principal shrine, hall and elevated superstructure.

Taranga also preserves evidence of earlier Buddhist religious activity in the wider hill area. This illustrates why a single sacred landscape may have remains belonging to more than one religious tradition and historical period.

Mount Abu and Jain marble architecture

The Dilwara Jain temples are located at Mount Abu in Rajasthan, not Gujarat. Their relevance to the architecture of western India lies especially in the richly carved marble interiors, pillars and ceilings.

Vimal Vasahi is associated with the patron Vimal Shah. Its comparatively restrained exterior and highly elaborate interior demonstrate the importance of internal sacred space in some Jain temples.

Other temples of the Dilwara complex belong to different patrons and periods. It would therefore be inaccurate to attribute the entire group to Vimal Shah.

How patronage shaped Jain architecture

Jain temple building was supported by rulers, merchants and wealthy lay devotees, as well as through community donations. Patronage made possible the quarrying, transport and carving of stone, the construction of halls and shrines, and later repair or enlargement.

The regional development of western Indian temple architecture is often described using the term Maru-Gurjara. Its elaborate structural and ornamental features appear across parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan. The term describes a regional architectural tradition, not a separate religion.

Prelims focus

  • Palitana is associated with Shatrunjaya Hill and Adinatha.
  • Girnar is in the Junagadh region and is associated with Neminatha.
  • Taranga in the Mehsana region has an important Ajitanatha temple.
  • The Taranga temple is associated with 12th-century Solanki patronage under Kumarapala.
  • Dilwara is at Mount Abu in Rajasthan; Vimal Vasahi is associated with Vimal Shah.
  • Trap: Palitana, Girnar and Taranga are in Gujarat, but Mount Abu is in Rajasthan.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 69–70 and 93–95; Gujarat Tourism, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill, Girnar Hill and Taranga Hill Jain Temple, site descriptions, consulted 23 November 2026; Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, District Census Handbook, Mehsana, historical description of Taranga.]

title: Structural Jain Temples and the Architectural Heritage of Gujarat

body:
How the architectural traditions differ

Harappan, Buddhist and Jain architecture can be distinguished most reliably by combining chronology, purpose, plan, architectural components and associated evidence. A building's shape alone may be insufficient because later traditions sometimes shared structural forms.

Tradition or formPrincipal purposeRecognition features
Harappan planned settlementUrban residence, movement and shared infrastructureGrid-pattern streets, drainage, standardised brickwork, fortified sections
Buddhist stupaRelic veneration and circumambulationAnda, harmika, yashti, chhatra, vedika and torana
Buddhist chaitya hallCongregational worshipEntered hall, often apsidal, with a stupa at the far end
Buddhist viharaMonastic residence and community activitiesCentral hall with surrounding cells; later examples may contain shrines
Jain rock-cut monastery or shrineMonastic residence or devotionExcavated cells, halls, carved Jain images and inscriptions
Structural Jain templeDevotion centred on Tirthankara imagesGarbhagriha, mandapa, shikhara and Jain iconography

There are similarities within these categories. Buddhist and Jain communities both used caves and structural shrines. Stupas are especially associated with Buddhism, but the mound form is not exclusively Buddhist in every historical context. Similarly, garbhagriha and mandapa are architectural terms shared across several Indian religious traditions.

Architecture, inscriptions and iconography as evidence

The purpose of a monument can be reconstructed through several kinds of evidence:

  • Plan and construction: A courtyard house, drainage channel, enclosed hall or shrine chamber indicates how a space could be used.
  • Objects and deposits: Relic caskets, seals, beads, tools and associated remains provide evidence for activities conducted at a site.
  • Inscriptions: Names of donors, religious affiliations or dedications may directly identify people and institutions connected with a monument.
  • Sculpture and symbols: Images and attributes may help establish a Buddhist or Jain association when interpreted in context.
  • Historical setting: Date, location and relation to surrounding buildings may support or limit a proposed explanation.

At Harappan sites, undeciphered writing restricts the certainty of some interpretations. At many early Buddhist and Jain sites, readable inscriptions provide more direct evidence about donors and religious institutions. Even then, surviving evidence may be incomplete.

Why conservation is essential

Conservation aims to protect the original material and historical information of monuments. In archaeological architecture, this includes preserving building foundations, wall alignments, water channels, sculptural fragments, inscriptions and the relationship between them.

Removing a carved panel from its original gateway may preserve the panel as an object while losing information about its placement. Similarly, rebuilding an ancient drain without recording its original construction may damage evidence about engineering techniques. Careful documentation and preservation of surviving material are therefore essential.

The contrasting histories of Sanchi and Amaravati show why preservation in situ is valuable. The history of brick removal at Harappa also shows how modern reuse of ancient building materials can irreversibly damage an archaeological site.

World Heritage recognition: status at the content cutoff

The following distinctions were confirmed against the UNESCO World Heritage Centre records at the content cutoff of 23 November 2026. The years refer to World Heritage inscription, except where a site is explicitly described as tentative.

SiteLocationUNESCO status
Ajanta CavesMaharashtraInscribed in 1983
Ellora CavesMaharashtraInscribed in 1983
Buddhist Monuments at SanchiMadhya PradeshInscribed in 1989
Mahabodhi Temple ComplexBiharInscribed in 2002
Nalanda MahaviharaBiharInscribed in 2016
Dholavira: a Harappan CityGujaratInscribed in 2021
Lothal port-town remainsGujaratTentative List submission in 2014

A World Heritage inscription means that the World Heritage Committee has added the property to the World Heritage List. A Tentative List identifies properties a country may consider for future nomination. Inclusion on a Tentative List is not a World Heritage inscription.

Applying the distinctions in prelims

A large brick-lined water tank on a Harappan citadel should first suggest the Great Bath at Mohenjodaro. Stone fortifications and extensive reservoirs in arid Kutch point towards Dholavira. A large basin beside a Gujarat Harappan settlement suggests Lothal, with the qualification that its dockyard function is interpreted.

For Buddhist monuments, a hemispherical relic mound suggests a stupa; an elongated worship hall containing a stupa suggests a chaitya-griha; and cells arranged around a common hall suggest a vihara. A Jain temple identification requires evidence such as a Tirthankara image, associated emblem or inscription rather than a generic temple tower alone.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan architecture is especially important for planned cities and civic water management.
  • Stupa, chaitya hall and vihara are distinct architectural forms.
  • Both Buddhist and Jain traditions developed rock-cut and structural monuments.
  • Architectural plans, inscriptions and iconography should be considered together.
  • Dholavira is an inscribed UNESCO property; Lothal remains on the Tentative List.
  • Trap: Shared architectural terms or building materials do not establish an identical religious function.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Themes 1 and 4, Bricks, Beads and Bones and Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 5–8, 23–24 and 95–107; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapters 4 and 6, pp. 35–47 and 69–95; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, World Heritage List entries for Ajanta, Ellora, Sanchi, Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Nalanda Mahavihara and Dholavira, and Tentative List entry 5918 for Lothal, inscription and submission records consulted 23 November 2026.]
